title: White nationalist demonstrators need to 'get out of our city,' Hamilton mayor says at 1st news conference

blocks.text: Hamilton

After a demonstration that witnesses said included pro-Nazi chants, Hamilton community leaders are calling for a city-wide response to white supremacy and anti-immigrant hate. New Mayor Keanin Loomis's first news conference addressed the issue.
Community leaders call for action after weekend demonstration with pro-Nazi chants
In response to a troubling demonstration last weekend, Hamilton community groups gathered outside city hall to call for action against white supremacy and anti-immigrant hate.
"I don’t think our belonging should be on the table for someone else to decide," Tehreem Zafar, director of health equity and newcomer services for YWCA Hamilton, told a news conference Thursday.
Nobody should have to justify their existence in the community, she said.
"No conditions. No fine print."

The news conference was held less than a week after a downtown demonstration involving about 20 to 25 people dressed in black and wearing masks. According to police and community members, they were shouting pro-Nazi comments.

In a weekend news release, the Hamilton Police Service said it was investigating the demonstration Saturday that began around 6 p.m. ET. Witnesses reported seeing participants carrying signs with the words "white only," police said.
Mayor urges people to contact police about demo

Zafar spoke alongside new Hamilton Mayor Keanin Loomis, Terri Bedminster of Refuge Newcomer Health, Grace Baldwin of the Hamilton Immigration Partnership Council (HIPC), Greg Dunnett of the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce, Anika Kuhnert of the advocacy group L’Association canadienne-française de l’Ontario (ACFO) Régionale Hamilton and Tariq Ismati of Wesley Urban Ministries.
City Councillors Maureen Wilson (Ward 1) and Cameron Kroetsch (Ward 2), and several police leaders, including Chief Frank Bergen, were also present.

items: Hamilton police investigate after witnesses report group shouting pro-Nazi comments at demonstration

blocks.text: In his first news conference as mayor following last month's municipal election, Loomis said he will use his position to strengthen anti-hate initiatives and support groups.
He said white nationalist demonstrators should "get out of our city," and urged anyone who knows who they are or has information about them to contact police.
"We simply cannot say hate has no home here and leave it at that."

"Who gave you the right" to determine who belongs in the city, Zafar asked of the demonstrators. She noted she was speaking on behalf of her organization, and as a Muslim, south Asian and Brown woman. Unless you're Indigenous, Zafar said, your ancestors came to Hamilton from somewhere else.
'We simply cannot say hate has no home here and leave it at that,' Loomis, left, told the news conference Thursday. (Justin Chandler/CBC)

Some of the same individuals and groups represented at the news conference Thursday were present in November 2024 to denounce hate after white nationalists demonstrated at Jackson Square with a banner calling for "mass deportations."

Hamilton has seen a "troubling rise in anti-immigrant sentiment" and a pattern of "anti-immigrant hate incidents," Bedminster said. She also referenced anti-immigration group Dominion Society, which announced it would host a conference in the region this past August. Community members rallied against that, too.
She said the Nov. 14 event was "another blatant act of white supremacy."
Group claims credit for the demonstration

A social media account claiming affiliation with Nationalist-13, also known as NS13, took credit for the demonstration. On the social media site X on Tuesday, it posted video showing a person speaking into a microphone outside a bank on King Street West, next to the Hamilton Street Railway bus terminal.

The speaker made the accusation that immigrants receive economic benefits in Canada while others in the country do not. They beseeched viewers to "embrace national socialism" and "the Aryan character." The video ends with members chanting. "Hail white Canada."
In videos and photos, Nationalist-13 members often hide their faces with masks printed with the Totenkopf, a death's head symbol used as an insignia by the Nazi SS.

items: Hamilton mayor asks residents to report hate after CBC traces white nationalist 'active clubs' to the city

blocks.text: NS13 is one of several white nationalist groups active in Hamilton and the region. In 2025, a CBC visual investigation identified members of the group who were training in a private Hamilton gym and at a public park.

Nationalist-13 has become more public in recent years, with masked members holding anti-immigration protests in the Ontario cities of Toronto, London and Hamilton. In February, group members stood outside Hamilton city hall, making Nazi salutes. During the October municipal election, the group targeted a Black city council candidate with a threatening social media comment.
NS13 members made Nazi salutes outside Hamilton city hall in February. (CBC)
Often, Zafar said, hate groups take people's economic worries, take them out of context and redirect them to target immigrants and racialized people. "We need to call it out," she said.
Ismati echoed Zafar's message, saying "the people we serve are not burdens. They're an asset."
A former refugee himself, Ismati said newcomers fill critical labour gaps and bring a lot of skills and knowledge. "When newcomers succeed, Hamilton succeeds."
Housing, affordability and economic insecurity deserve serious conversations, not scapegoats, Dunnett, said, adding that the city can't be open for business if people don't feel safe in it.

Tehreem Zafar, director of health equity and newcomer services for YWCA Hamilton, says hate groups twist people's real economic anxieties to target immigrants and racialized people. (Justin Chandler/CBC)
Proactive response needed

At the news conference, speakers said it's important to go beyond condemning white supremacy. Baldwin, HIPC's chair, said community members should support one another, challenge hate and misinformation, and be prepared to have tough conversations.

Bedminster called on residents, businesses, institutions and politicians to speak out where they can, reflect on how to make Hamilton more welcoming, and report incidents of hate when they see them. She highlighted anti-hate resources people can access from groups including No Hate in the Hammer and the city-backed Hamilton For All campaign.

blocks.text: After Loomis's news conference, Kuhnert told CBC Hamilton she feels the city's francophone community is being included in anti-hate discussions more now than in the past. That's important because many of the city's French speakers are racialized.

Kuhnert added that the ACFO is seeking funding from the Department of Canadian Heritage to translate the community-run We Support Hamilton hate incident reporting tool into French so more people can use it.

The Hamilton Anti-Racism Resource Centre, which administers that tool, is hosting a community discussion at the Workers Arts and Heritage Centre this Saturday, with a focus on anti-racist approaches to public safety.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Justin Chandler is a CBC News reporter in Hamilton. He covers stories of all kinds from places including picket lines, court rooms, council meetings and research labs. Justin has a special interest in how public policy affects people, and loves a quirky human-interest story. Before CBC Hamilton, he worked for TVO and on a variety of CBC teams and programs. He co-hosted Radio Free Krypton on Met Radio.
